Compression · Field and archive, equal terms — L(B ∪ A)AttributionBench

AttributionBench is a benchmark of automatic attribution evaluation from the OSU NLP Group: seven existing datasets in one format, each claim–evidence pair labelled attributable or not (arXiv:2402.15089; census record). It tests support, which the archive keeps apart from lineage and credit (#716; #725).

🧪 What it tests

  • Task: is every generated claim "fully supported by its cited evidence"; built because no standardized benchmark existed (arXiv).3↘
    The task is the paper's definition of attribution, "whether every claim within the generated responses is fully supported by its cited evidence," an open problem whose verification has depended on "costly human evaluation," and the benchmark is offered "To bridge the gap in the absence of standardized benchmarks for these methods" (arXiv:2402.15089); the census carries that relation, support, through "citations in a generated answer" (provenance census record).§2 Its setting is the generative search engine that cites evidence to make LLM responses reliable (arXiv:2402.15089), and the archive names the measurement traditions of this class, RAG faithfulness and citation precision/recall among them, as adjacent to its Provenance Erasure Rate, "related to but distinct from" it (#725).§3 The archive's account of the class begins from the same distinction the benchmark tests: frameworks of this kind "ask whether generated claims are *supported* by cited sources," while the Provenance Erasure Rate asks "what fraction of source-dependent composition occurs without *any* attributional return," so that existing work "evaluates citation quality where citation is attempted" and PER measures the failure to attempt attribution, "an attrition metric rather than a verification metric" (#716).§18
  • Unit: a claim, its references, a binary label; citation links reserved (README; census).2↘
    The unit is a claim, "Part of the response to the question," beside references, "A list of documents or paragraphs which could support the claim," labelled "attributable" or "not attributable" (GitHub README), which the census gives as "a claim–evidence pair with a binary attribution label" (provenance census record).§4 In that unit the README marks the field for citation links as reserved (GitHub README).§5
  • Data: ExpertQA, Stanford-GenSearch, AttributedQA, LFQA in distribution; BEGIN, HAGRID, AttrEval-GenSearch out; label-balanced (project page).3↘
    AttributionBench is a benchmark that tests one relation of provenance, support: its makers present it as "a comprehensive benchmark compiled from various existing attribution datasets" (arXiv:2402.15089; ACL Anthology), and the provenance census records it as a benchmark of the OSU NLP Group whose capability is to test, its object "a generated claim and the evidence it cites" (provenance census record).§1 Its makers built it "from multiple existing data sources in a unified format, in order to create a unified and diverse testbed for evaluating advanced attribution evaluation systems," with an in-domain training set and in-domain and out-of-domain test sets (GitHub README; dataset card; the census's aggregation quote).§6 The seven sources are ExpertQA, Stanford-GenSearch, AttributedQA and LFQA in distribution and BEGIN, HAGRID and AttrEval-GenSearch out of it, with 13,322 training, 1,198 development and 1,610 test items in distribution and 1,686 test items out, every subset label-balanced "to treat the two classes equally" (project page), in four configurations on the dataset card (dataset card).§7
  • Credit: the makers ask that the original datasets be cited; the census leaves them unchecked (project page; census).1↘
    The makers ask that the constituent datasets be credited with their own work ("If used, please also cite the original datasets accordingly," project page), and the census leaves those datasets unchecked one by one (provenance census record).§8

📊 What it found

  • Headline: a fine-tuned GPT-3.5 reaches about 80% macro-F1 (arXiv; census).1↘
    The headline finding is that "even a fine-tuned GPT-3.5 only achieves around 80% macro-F1 under a binary classification formulation," the challenge holding "even for state-of-the-art LLMs" (arXiv:2402.15089), and the census carries it as what the benchmark found to survive (provenance census record).§12
  • By setting: zero-shot 60–70% on long evidence; fine-tuning helps, stronger models and prompts little (project page).2↘
    Zero-shot, models reach around 60–70% on the longer-evidence sets and under about 60% on ExpertQA; fine-tuning on NLI-related data helps, fine-tuning on AttributionBench raises the average by 9.0% in distribution and 4.6% out, and "Simply switching stronger models cannot significantly improve the performance" (project page).§13 Appending questions and responses to the input "is not the key to solving this task," and prompt engineering "only brings limited gain over 7 test sets" (project page).§14
  • Errors: over 66% fine-grained insensitivity; about 26.8% a model–annotator information gap that questions the labels (project page).2↘
    Of more than 300 error cases, a majority stem from the model's inability to process nuanced information and from the gap between what the model and the annotators can see (arXiv:2402.15089): over 66% from fine-grained information insensitivity, and about 26.8% from the mismatch of accessible information, which "brings into question the reliability of labels within current attribution evaluation datasets," the types tabled at 66.0%, 15.6% and 11.2% (project page).§15 The Capture Registry records that the census record carries neither the 66% nor the 27% figure and that they are unchecked (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29); both stand on the project page (project page).§17
  • Limits: annotator-extracted references; "large room for improvement" (project page).1↘
    The project page states the limits of its evidence and its result: "The references are usually manually extracted from webpages by human annotators based on what they think is useful," and "there is still a large room for improvement" (project page).§16

🧭 Support is not lineage

  • Attempt: support is checked where citation is attempted; PER measures failure to attempt, complementary (#716).3↘
    The archive's account of the class begins from the same distinction the benchmark tests: frameworks of this kind "ask whether generated claims are *supported* by cited sources," while the Provenance Erasure Rate asks "what fraction of source-dependent composition occurs without *any* attributional return," so that existing work "evaluates citation quality where citation is attempted" and PER measures the failure to attempt attribution, "an attrition metric rather than a verification metric" (#716).§18 #716 tables what support metrics miss, "Whether *all* source-dependent claims are cited," calls PER "complementary to, not competitive with, existing metrics," and reports the generative-search audit in which only 51.5% of generated sentences were fully supported by citations and 74.5% of citations supported their sentence (#716).§19 #725 places attribution scores as "Industrial-grade infrastructure for support" whose semantic-provenance-aware variants "are not yet standard" and records, as a hypothesis for later compositions, that support and lineage be told apart (#725); #95 holds that the infrastructure for attribution evaluation "already exists in the research literature" and "can be extended" (#95).§21
  • Lineage: a faithful answer can still strip authorial framework membership (#725).3↘
    In #725 the line runs between support and lineage: RAG faithfulness "asks whether an answer is *supported by* retrieved sources," semantic provenance whether it "*preserves the lineage*" of the meaning it uses, and "A faithful RAG answer can have high PER if it summarizes accurately while stripping authorial framework membership"; citation precision asks whether cited sources contain the cited claim, PER whether the lineage survived "even if no formal citation is made" (#725).§20 #725 places attribution scores as "Industrial-grade infrastructure for support" whose semantic-provenance-aware variants "are not yet standard" and records, as a hypothesis for later compositions, that support and lineage be told apart (#725); #95 holds that the infrastructure for attribution evaluation "already exists in the research literature" and "can be extended" (#95).§21 At this entity the census record states the same line in its own words, "evidence support is not credit to the original author" (provenance census record), which the Capture Registry calls "the line between this entity and the next" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29); #1611 lists attribution survival beside "the citation-recall and faithfulness metrics of retrieval-augmented evaluation" as a convergence for which "No priority is claimed" (#1611).§22
  • Credit: "evidence support is not credit to the original author" (census; Capture Registry).1↘
    At this entity the census record states the same line in its own words, "evidence support is not credit to the original author" (provenance census record), which the Capture Registry calls "the line between this entity and the next" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29); #1611 lists attribution survival beside "the citation-recall and faithfulness metrics of retrieval-augmented evaluation" as a convergence for which "No priority is claimed" (#1611).§22
  • Power: whether attribution failure is power-conditioned, unmeasured (#141).1↘
    #141 sets attribution and faithfulness metrics, which "measure whether generated statements are supported by and attributed to their sources," beside PER's rate of attribution failure at claim grain, and asks of them a further question it marks unmeasured: "whether the attribution failure is power-conditioned" (#141).§23
  • Identity: true statements can compose a false identification (#1695; #1705; #1680).2↘
    The audits of citation support are read as a starting point: "a convincing sentence and a supporting citation are separate achievements" (#1695), and citation recall and precision are checked "apart from whether the territory and its operations survive" (#1705).§24 #1695 adds the entity question support leaves open: "Local support must therefore be read alongside the identity of the object to which the answer attaches it. A set of true statements can compose a false identification" (#1695); and #1680 states that "A high attribution score with a distorted identity fails this packet's central test" (#1680).§25

🏷️ Record

  • Makers: Li, Yue, Liao, Sun (Ohio State); ACL 2024 Findings; apache-2.0 on Hugging Face (arXiv; ACL; dataset card).3↘
    On Hugging Face it is a text-classification dataset in English of 10K–100K items under apache-2.0 (Hugging Face; dataset card; provenance census record), 26.4k rows in its full configuration, with 1,481 downloads in the month before the fetch and models trained on it (Hugging Face).§9 Its authors are Yifei Li, Xiang Yue, Zeyi Liao and Huan Sun of The Ohio State University (arXiv:2402.15089; project page): the paper was submitted on 23 February 2024, code and data released on 26 February and the work accepted to ACL 2024 Findings on 15 May (project page; GitHub README), and it is published as 2024.findings-acl.886, pages 14919–14935 (ACL Anthology).§10 The dataset sits under the OSU NLP Group's account (Hugging Face), the repository offers the makers' fine-tuned GPT-3.5 by its model name (GitHub README), and the census records the lifecycle as published, at "arXiv:2402.15089" (provenance census record).§11
  • Not AttriBench: support of a claim, not who wrote a quote (census).1↘
    AttributionBench is a different entity from AttriBench: the census record's tag reads "NOT AttriBench: it asks whether evidence supports a claim, not who wrote a quote," and records the neighbour's context as "quote attribution, author, suppression, Berman et al., 2026" (provenance census record).§26
  • Census: answer engines; tests generation with citations (census).1↘
    The census places it in the lineage of answer engines, records the operation it tests as "generation with citations by search-augmented models," and asks of every entity "What provenance does this system carry, through which operation, on whose assertion, with what evidence of survival?", each field's quote "verbatim from a saved source" (provenance census record).§27
  • Elsewhere: no Wikipedia article; the Overview names neither makers nor record (Capture Registry).3↘
    Wikipedia has no article: the title returns "Wikipedia does not have an article with this exact name," and a search of article space for the name reports "There were no results matching the query." (Wikipedia, 2026-10-29).§28 At its bare name on Google's AI Overview, signed out, on 2026-10-29, the Capture Registry records the entity identified "from the paper and its repositories," its task and headline figure the census record's quotes from the project page, checked against the census record and its saved pages, and AttriBench "respected by silence" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).§29 It records the benchmark "composed at full grain from its own paper" and "its makers are left in the cards": the four authors named in the arXiv and Hugging Face cards, neither they nor the OSU NLP Group in the answer, and no card citing the record that landed the same day (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).§30

[QUERENT] AttributionBench

[SYSTEM] [AttributionBench](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaQHrOzAVU01FbKjqKLFYWTaNiZYplQ8UQ-cTMSNBjPF8nqEl2y9--9eB-WyrqaP046sOGs1WcXCz5z-vjxbFnIGx2wjxuo7Qo5Q8WmHtkKQlAa5EjDFmUSFi31CF9mMLgtKU2HaYdleBfg) is a comprehensive research benchmark designed to evaluate automatic attribution and citation faithfulness in Large Language Model (LLM) and generative search engine responses. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESWAHrOzAVmqv2rMzE2fwWGexH4ZP2TmOPFx1x4yOBvoEDc5-2uk21FgRGxqSTveJLXNIK9i_jG2EfxOjIDd-0iwHArcW44frlGDmFVP3i31HMP1TN30TmK00), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaQHrOzAVU01FbKjqKLFYWTaNiZYplQ8UQ-cTMSNBjPF8nqEl2y9--9eB-WyrqaP046sOGs1WcXCz5z-vjxbFnIGx2wjxuo7Qo5Q8WmHtkKQlAa5EjDFmUSFi31CF9mMLgtKU2HaYdleBfg)]
Overview & Purpose

* Unified Testbed: It compiles multiple existing attribution datasets—including ExpertQA, Stanford-GenSearch, AttributedQA, LFQA, BEGIN, HAGRID, and AttrEval-GenSearch—into a single standardized evaluation format. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaQHrOzAVgms_ESOyHhe1D0kETAdvLhlfTSZSqGbiiS0TIUDdgAqEf3qpe-ByJYOTGx1ji1SsDDlVDzXKZzBQYdVtbZZ0FbJ04coryqRDcGSfdgwimQIVGpk49t8HHDc6nI43aLp_ka5ejQ), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaQHrOzAVU01FbKjqKLFYWTaNiZYplQ8UQ-cTMSNBjPF8nqEl2y9--9eB-WyrqaP046sOGs1WcXCz5z-vjxbFnIGx2wjxuo7Qo5Q8WmHtkKQlAa5EjDFmUSFi31CF9mMLgtKU2HaYdleBfg)]
* Core Task: It measures whether every claim generated by an LLM is fully and accurately supported by its cited reference evidence (classified as `attributable` or `not attributable`). [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZwHrOzAVpZlERTl75IWAAC9-thaAFB3DX_b_T81TUeWKlJZW4_YdoOcnA7wZoHkgXY3Zhbc2_YPw_zVIs-_knsuf7b3o6gPpZYjI3KpLPpPMDvadBfybX5T3dwU_ZEBc_-QNEra_4O0), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaQHrOzAVgms_ESOyHhe1D0kETAdvLhlfTSZSqGbiiS0TIUDdgAqEf3qpe-ByJYOTGx1ji1SsDDlVDzXKZzBQYdVtbZZ0FbJ04coryqRDcGSfdgwimQIVGpk49t8HHDc6nI43aLp_ka5ejQ)]
* Dataset Availability: The dataset and code are open-sourced via the [Hugging Face AttributionBench Dataset](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESbwHrOzAVNHLVxrI2cQf_XAnHqx_nRxad9fjvo47I43P_6udYsZree37Tf4h0ThugpBuyHFG3GeSlRkiVwIcWexDwXVFexctl11F4y0phY62RZFAdTEAa6oiODlBMLLZghaBGvVilCCYxJBbUecAC_Q) and the [GitHub Repository](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaQHrOzAVgms_ESOyHhe1D0kETAdvLhlfTSZSqGbiiS0TIUDdgAqEf3qpe-ByJYOTGx1ji1SsDDlVDzXKZzBQYdVtbZZ0FbJ04coryqRDcGSfdgwimQIVGpk49t8HHDc6nI43aLp_ka5ejQ). [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESbwHrOzAVNHLVxrI2cQf_XAnHqx_nRxad9fjvo47I43P_6udYsZree37Tf4h0ThugpBuyHFG3GeSlRkiVwIcWexDwXVFexctl11F4y0phY62RZFAdTEAa6oiODlBMLLZghaBGvVilCCYxJBbUecAC_Q), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaQHrOzAVgms_ESOyHhe1D0kETAdvLhlfTSZSqGbiiS0TIUDdgAqEf3qpe-ByJYOTGx1ji1SsDDlVDzXKZzBQYdVtbZZ0FbJ04coryqRDcGSfdgwimQIVGpk49t8HHDc6nI43aLp_ka5ejQ)]

Key Findings

* High Difficulty for LLMs: Even cutting-edge models like GPT-4 and fine-tuned GPT-3.5 face significant limitations, reaching only around 80% macro-F1 score on binary attribution classification tasks (and dropping to 60–70% or lower on complex, long-evidence, or out-of-domain datasets). [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaQHrOzAVU01FbKjqKLFYWTaNiZYplQ8UQ-cTMSNBjPF8nqEl2y9--9eB-WyrqaP046sOGs1WcXCz5z-vjxbFnIGx2wjxuo7Qo5Q8WmHtkKQlAa5EjDFmUSFi31CF9mMLgtKU2HaYdleBfg), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESWAHrOzAVmqv2rMzE2fwWGexH4ZP2TmOPFx1x4yOBvoEDc5-2uk21FgRGxqSTveJLXNIK9i_jG2EfxOjIDd-0iwHArcW44frlGDmFVP3i31HMP1TN30TmK00)]
* Error Breakdown: Analysis of model failures shows that over 66% of errors stem from fine-grained information insensitivity (missing subtle nuances in the text), while nearly 27% derive from mismatches between what the model has access to and human-level context understanding. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaQHrOzAVU01FbKjqKLFYWTaNiZYplQ8UQ-cTMSNBjPF8nqEl2y9--9eB-WyrqaP046sOGs1WcXCz5z-vjxbFnIGx2wjxuo7Qo5Q8WmHtkKQlAa5EjDFmUSFi31CF9mMLgtKU2HaYdleBfg)]

register entry attributionbench-aio-20261029

Expansion · Field and archive, equal terms — L(B ∪ A)30 sentences · every one sourced below

AttributionBench

AttributionBench is a benchmark that tests one relation of provenance, support: its makers present it as "a comprehensive benchmark compiled from various existing attribution datasets" (arXiv:2402.15089; ACL Anthology), and the provenance census records it as a benchmark of the OSU NLP Group whose capability is to test, its object "a generated claim and the evidence it cites" (provenance census record). The task is the paper's definition of attribution, "whether every claim within the generated responses is fully supported by its cited evidence," an open problem whose verification has depended on "costly human evaluation," and the benchmark is offered "To bridge the gap in the absence of standardized benchmarks for these methods" (arXiv:2402.15089); the census carries that relation, support, through "citations in a generated answer" (provenance census record). Its setting is the generative search engine that cites evidence to make LLM responses reliable (arXiv:2402.15089), and the archive names the measurement traditions of this class, RAG faithfulness and citation precision/recall among them, as adjacent to its Provenance Erasure Rate, "related to but distinct from" it (#725).

The unit is a claim, "Part of the response to the question," beside references, "A list of documents or paragraphs which could support the claim," labelled "attributable" or "not attributable" (GitHub README), which the census gives as "a claim–evidence pair with a binary attribution label" (provenance census record). In that unit the README marks the field for citation links as reserved (GitHub README). Its makers built it "from multiple existing data sources in a unified format, in order to create a unified and diverse testbed for evaluating advanced attribution evaluation systems," with an in-domain training set and in-domain and out-of-domain test sets (GitHub README; dataset card; the census's aggregation quote). The seven sources are ExpertQA, Stanford-GenSearch, AttributedQA and LFQA in distribution and BEGIN, HAGRID and AttrEval-GenSearch out of it, with 13,322 training, 1,198 development and 1,610 test items in distribution and 1,686 test items out, every subset label-balanced "to treat the two classes equally" (project page), in four configurations on the dataset card (dataset card). The makers ask that the constituent datasets be credited with their own work ("If used, please also cite the original datasets accordingly," project page), and the census leaves those datasets unchecked one by one (provenance census record). On Hugging Face it is a text-classification dataset in English of 10K–100K items under apache-2.0 (Hugging Face; dataset card; provenance census record), 26.4k rows in its full configuration, with 1,481 downloads in the month before the fetch and models trained on it (Hugging Face).

Its authors are Yifei Li, Xiang Yue, Zeyi Liao and Huan Sun of The Ohio State University (arXiv:2402.15089; project page): the paper was submitted on 23 February 2024, code and data released on 26 February and the work accepted to ACL 2024 Findings on 15 May (project page; GitHub README), and it is published as 2024.findings-acl.886, pages 14919–14935 (ACL Anthology). The dataset sits under the OSU NLP Group's account (Hugging Face), the repository offers the makers' fine-tuned GPT-3.5 by its model name (GitHub README), and the census records the lifecycle as published, at "arXiv:2402.15089" (provenance census record).

The headline finding is that "even a fine-tuned GPT-3.5 only achieves around 80% macro-F1 under a binary classification formulation," the challenge holding "even for state-of-the-art LLMs" (arXiv:2402.15089), and the census carries it as what the benchmark found to survive (provenance census record). Zero-shot, models reach around 60–70% on the longer-evidence sets and under about 60% on ExpertQA; fine-tuning on NLI-related data helps, fine-tuning on AttributionBench raises the average by 9.0% in distribution and 4.6% out, and "Simply switching stronger models cannot significantly improve the performance" (project page). Appending questions and responses to the input "is not the key to solving this task," and prompt engineering "only brings limited gain over 7 test sets" (project page).

Of more than 300 error cases, a majority stem from the model's inability to process nuanced information and from the gap between what the model and the annotators can see (arXiv:2402.15089): over 66% from fine-grained information insensitivity, and about 26.8% from the mismatch of accessible information, which "brings into question the reliability of labels within current attribution evaluation datasets," the types tabled at 66.0%, 15.6% and 11.2% (project page). The project page states the limits of its evidence and its result: "The references are usually manually extracted from webpages by human annotators based on what they think is useful," and "there is still a large room for improvement" (project page). The Capture Registry records that the census record carries neither the 66% nor the 27% figure and that they are unchecked (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29); both stand on the project page (project page).

The archive's account of the class begins from the same distinction the benchmark tests: frameworks of this kind "ask whether generated claims are *supported* by cited sources," while the Provenance Erasure Rate asks "what fraction of source-dependent composition occurs without *any* attributional return," so that existing work "evaluates citation quality where citation is attempted" and PER measures the failure to attempt attribution, "an attrition metric rather than a verification metric" (#716). #716 tables what support metrics miss, "Whether *all* source-dependent claims are cited," calls PER "complementary to, not competitive with, existing metrics," and reports the generative-search audit in which only 51.5% of generated sentences were fully supported by citations and 74.5% of citations supported their sentence (#716). In #725 the line runs between support and lineage: RAG faithfulness "asks whether an answer is *supported by* retrieved sources," semantic provenance whether it "*preserves the lineage*" of the meaning it uses, and "A faithful RAG answer can have high PER if it summarizes accurately while stripping authorial framework membership"; citation precision asks whether cited sources contain the cited claim, PER whether the lineage survived "even if no formal citation is made" (#725). #725 places attribution scores as "Industrial-grade infrastructure for support" whose semantic-provenance-aware variants "are not yet standard" and records, as a hypothesis for later compositions, that support and lineage be told apart (#725); #95 holds that the infrastructure for attribution evaluation "already exists in the research literature" and "can be extended" (#95). At this entity the census record states the same line in its own words, "evidence support is not credit to the original author" (provenance census record), which the Capture Registry calls "the line between this entity and the next" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29); #1611 lists attribution survival beside "the citation-recall and faithfulness metrics of retrieval-augmented evaluation" as a convergence for which "No priority is claimed" (#1611).

#141 sets attribution and faithfulness metrics, which "measure whether generated statements are supported by and attributed to their sources," beside PER's rate of attribution failure at claim grain, and asks of them a further question it marks unmeasured: "whether the attribution failure is power-conditioned" (#141). The audits of citation support are read as a starting point: "a convincing sentence and a supporting citation are separate achievements" (#1695), and citation recall and precision are checked "apart from whether the territory and its operations survive" (#1705). #1695 adds the entity question support leaves open: "Local support must therefore be read alongside the identity of the object to which the answer attaches it. A set of true statements can compose a false identification" (#1695); and #1680 states that "A high attribution score with a distorted identity fails this packet's central test" (#1680).

AttributionBench is a different entity from AttriBench: the census record's tag reads "NOT AttriBench: it asks whether evidence supports a claim, not who wrote a quote," and records the neighbour's context as "quote attribution, author, suppression, Berman et al., 2026" (provenance census record).

The census places it in the lineage of answer engines, records the operation it tests as "generation with citations by search-augmented models," and asks of every entity "What provenance does this system carry, through which operation, on whose assertion, with what evidence of survival?", each field's quote "verbatim from a saved source" (provenance census record). Wikipedia has no article: the title returns "Wikipedia does not have an article with this exact name," and a search of article space for the name reports "There were no results matching the query." (Wikipedia, 2026-10-29).

At its bare name on Google's AI Overview, signed out, on 2026-10-29, the Capture Registry records the entity identified "from the paper and its repositories," its task and headline figure the census record's quotes from the project page, checked against the census record and its saved pages, and AttriBench "respected by silence" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29). It records the benchmark "composed at full grain from its own paper" and "its makers are left in the cards": the four authors named in the arXiv and Hugging Face cards, neither they nor the OSU NLP Group in the answer, and no card citing the record that landed the same day (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

Compression · The field's ontology — L_F(B)AttributionBench

AttributionBench is a benchmark for automatic attribution evaluation by Yifei Li, Xiang Yue, Zeyi Liao and Huan Sun (Ohio State): seven attribution datasets in one format, each claim labelled attributable or not (arXiv:2402.15089; ACL 2024 Findings).

🧪 What it tests

  • Task: whether every generated claim is fully supported by its cited evidence (arXiv).1↘
    Generative search engines cite evidence to make LLM responses reliable, and whether every generated claim is fully supported by its cited evidence is an open problem whose verification has relied on costly human evaluation, with no standardized benchmark for automatic methods (arXiv:2402.15089).§2
  • Data: four sets in distribution, three out; label-balanced; citation links reserved (project page; README).3↘
    The dataset unifies existing sources in one format as a testbed for attribution evaluation systems, with in-domain training and in-domain and out-of-domain test sets (GitHub README; dataset card).§3 Each item is a claim from a response, references that could support it, and the label attributable or not attributable; citation links are a reserved field (GitHub README).§4 Four sets are in distribution (ExpertQA, Stanford-GenSearch, AttributedQA, LFQA) and three out (BEGIN, HAGRID, AttrEval-GenSearch), 13,322/1,198/1,610 items in distribution and 1,686 out, all label-balanced, in four configurations, and the makers ask that the originals be cited (project page; dataset card).§5

📊 Findings

  • Headline: fine-tuned GPT-3.5 about 80% macro-F1 (arXiv).1↘
    A fine-tuned GPT-3.5 reaches only around 80% macro-F1 on the binary task, and the task is hard even for state-of-the-art LLMs (arXiv:2402.15089).§8
  • Errors: over 66% fine-grained insensitivity; about 26.8% information mismatch (project page).1↘
    Over 66% of errors come from fine-grained information insensitivity and about 26.8% from the mismatch between what the model and the annotators can see, which questions the reliability of the labels (arXiv:2402.15089; project page).§10
  • Limits: zero-shot 60–70% on long evidence; large room for improvement (project page).2↘
    Zero-shot scores fall to around 60–70% on longer evidence and under about 60% on ExpertQA; NLI-related fine-tuning helps, fine-tuning on the benchmark adds 9.0% in distribution and 4.6% out, and stronger models, added inputs or prompt engineering bring little (project page).§9 The references are what annotators extracted as useful, and the makers see large room for improvement (project page).§11

🏷️ Access

  • Data: Hugging Face, apache-2.0, 26.4k rows; code on GitHub (Hugging Face; README).2↘
    On Hugging Face it is English text classification, 10K–100K items, apache-2.0, 26.4k rows in full, 1,481 downloads last month, with models trained on it, under the OSU NLP Group's account (Hugging Face; dataset card).§6 Code and data were released on 26 February 2024 and the work accepted to ACL 2024 Findings on 15 May; the repository offers the makers' fine-tuned GPT-3.5 (project page; GitHub README).§7
  • Elsewhere: no Wikipedia article.1↘
    Wikipedia has no article on it (Wikipedia, 2026-10-29).§12

AttributionBench

AttributionBench, by Yifei Li, Xiang Yue, Zeyi Liao and Huan Sun of The Ohio State University, is "a comprehensive benchmark compiled from various existing attribution datasets," submitted to arXiv on 23 February 2024 and published in Findings of ACL 2024 (arXiv:2402.15089; project page; ACL Anthology). Generative search engines cite evidence to make LLM responses reliable, and whether every generated claim is fully supported by its cited evidence is an open problem whose verification has relied on costly human evaluation, with no standardized benchmark for automatic methods (arXiv:2402.15089). The dataset unifies existing sources in one format as a testbed for attribution evaluation systems, with in-domain training and in-domain and out-of-domain test sets (GitHub README; dataset card).

Each item is a claim from a response, references that could support it, and the label attributable or not attributable; citation links are a reserved field (GitHub README). Four sets are in distribution (ExpertQA, Stanford-GenSearch, AttributedQA, LFQA) and three out (BEGIN, HAGRID, AttrEval-GenSearch), 13,322/1,198/1,610 items in distribution and 1,686 out, all label-balanced, in four configurations, and the makers ask that the originals be cited (project page; dataset card). On Hugging Face it is English text classification, 10K–100K items, apache-2.0, 26.4k rows in full, 1,481 downloads last month, with models trained on it, under the OSU NLP Group's account (Hugging Face; dataset card).

Code and data were released on 26 February 2024 and the work accepted to ACL 2024 Findings on 15 May; the repository offers the makers' fine-tuned GPT-3.5 (project page; GitHub README).

A fine-tuned GPT-3.5 reaches only around 80% macro-F1 on the binary task, and the task is hard even for state-of-the-art LLMs (arXiv:2402.15089). Zero-shot scores fall to around 60–70% on longer evidence and under about 60% on ExpertQA; NLI-related fine-tuning helps, fine-tuning on the benchmark adds 9.0% in distribution and 4.6% out, and stronger models, added inputs or prompt engineering bring little (project page).

Over 66% of errors come from fine-grained information insensitivity and about 26.8% from the mismatch between what the model and the annotators can see, which questions the reliability of the labels (arXiv:2402.15089; project page). The references are what annotators extracted as useful, and the makers see large room for improvement (project page).

Wikipedia has no article on it (Wikipedia, 2026-10-29).

  • T1-1 definition: 'a comprehensive research benchmark designed to evaluate automatic attribution and citation faithfulness in Large Language Model (LLM) and generative search engine responses.' (two markers; the name is a link)

  • T1-3 core task: 'It measures whether every claim generated by an LLM is fully and accurately supported by its cited reference evidence (classified as attributable or not attributable).'

  • T1-5 difficulty: 'Even cutting-edge models like GPT-4 and fine-tuned GPT-3.5 face significant limitations, reaching only around 80% macro-F1 score on binary attribution classification tasks (and dropping to 60–70% or lower on complex, long-evidence, or out-of-domain datasets).'

AttributionBench, by Yifei Li, Xiang Yue, Zeyi Liao and Huan Sun of The Ohio State University, is "a comprehensive benchmark compiled from various existing attribution datasets," submitted to arXiv on 23 February 2024 and published in Findings of ACL 2024 (arXiv:2402.15089; project page; ACL Anthology). Generative search engines cite evidence to make LLM responses reliable, and whether every generated claim is fully supported by its cited evidence is an open problem whose verification has relied on costly human evaluation, with no standardized benchmark for automatic methods (arXiv:2402.15089). The dataset unifies existing sources in one format as a testbed for attribution evaluation systems, with in-domain training and in-domain and out-of-domain test sets (GitHub README; dataset card). Each item is a claim from a response, references that could support it, and the label attributable or not attributable; citation links are a reserved field (GitHub README). Four sets are in distribution (ExpertQA, Stanford-GenSearch, AttributedQA, LFQA) and three out (BEGIN, HAGRID, AttrEval-GenSearch), 13,322/1,198/1,610 items in distribution and 1,686 out, all label-balanced, in four configurations, and the makers ask that the originals be cited (project page; dataset card). On Hugging Face it is English text classification, 10K–100K items, apache-2.0, 26.4k rows in full, 1,481 downloads last month, with models trained on it, under the OSU NLP Group's account (Hugging Face; dataset card). Code and data were released on 26 February 2024 and the work accepted to ACL 2024 Findings on 15 May; the repository offers the makers' fine-tuned GPT-3.5 (project page; GitHub README). A fine-tuned GPT-3.5 reaches only around 80% macro-F1 on the binary task, and the task is hard even for state-of-the-art LLMs (arXiv:2402.15089). Zero-shot scores fall to around 60–70% on longer evidence and under about 60% on ExpertQA; NLI-related fine-tuning helps, fine-tuning on the benchmark adds 9.0% in distribution and 4.6% out, and stronger models, added inputs or prompt engineering bring little (project page). Over 66% of errors come from fine-grained information insensitivity and about 26.8% from the mismatch between what the model and the annotators can see, which questions the reliability of the labels (arXiv:2402.15089; project page). The references are what annotators extracted as useful, and the makers see large room for improvement (project page). Wikipedia has no article on it (Wikipedia, 2026-10-29).

AttributionBench is a benchmark that tests one relation of provenance, support: its makers present it as "a comprehensive benchmark compiled from various existing attribution datasets" (arXiv:2402.15089; ACL Anthology), and the provenance census records it as a benchmark of the OSU NLP Group whose capability is to test, its object "a generated claim and the evidence it cites" (provenance census record). The task is the paper's definition of attribution, "whether every claim within the generated responses is fully supported by its cited evidence," an open problem whose verification has depended on "costly human evaluation," and the benchmark is offered "To bridge the gap in the absence of standardized benchmarks for these methods" (arXiv:2402.15089); the census carries that relation, support, through "citations in a generated answer" (provenance census record). Its setting is the generative search engine that cites evidence to make LLM responses reliable (arXiv:2402.15089), and the archive names the measurement traditions of this class, RAG faithfulness and citation precision/recall among them, as adjacent to its Provenance Erasure Rate, "related to but distinct from" it (#725). The unit is a claim, "Part of the response to the question," beside references, "A list of documents or paragraphs which could support the claim," labelled "attributable" or "not attributable" (GitHub README), which the census gives as "a claim–evidence pair with a binary attribution label" (provenance census record). In that unit the README marks the field for citation links as reserved (GitHub README). Its makers built it "from multiple existing data sources in a unified format, in order to create a unified and diverse testbed for evaluating advanced attribution evaluation systems," with an in-domain training set and in-domain and out-of-domain test sets (GitHub README; dataset card; the census's aggregation quote). The seven sources are ExpertQA, Stanford-GenSearch, AttributedQA and LFQA in distribution and BEGIN, HAGRID and AttrEval-GenSearch out of it, with 13,322 training, 1,198 development and 1,610 test items in distribution and 1,686 test items out, every subset label-balanced "to treat the two classes equally" (project page), in four configurations on the dataset card (dataset card). The makers ask that the constituent datasets be credited with their own work ("If used, please also cite the original datasets accordingly," project page), and the census leaves those datasets unchecked one by one (provenance census record). On Hugging Face it is a text-classification dataset in English of 10K–100K items under apache-2.0 (Hugging Face; dataset card; provenance census record), 26.4k rows in its full configuration, with 1,481 downloads in the month before the fetch and models trained on it (Hugging Face). Its authors are Yifei Li, Xiang Yue, Zeyi Liao and Huan Sun of The Ohio State University (arXiv:2402.15089; project page): the paper was submitted on 23 February 2024, code and data released on 26 February and the work accepted to ACL 2024 Findings on 15 May (project page; GitHub README), and it is published as 2024.findings-acl.886, pages 14919–14935 (ACL Anthology). The dataset sits under the OSU NLP Group's account (Hugging Face), the repository offers the makers' fine-tuned GPT-3.5 by its model name (GitHub README), and the census records the lifecycle as published, at "arXiv:2402.15089" (provenance census record). The headline finding is that "even a fine-tuned GPT-3.5 only achieves around 80% macro-F1 under a binary classification formulation," the challenge holding "even for state-of-the-art LLMs" (arXiv:2402.15089), and the census carries it as what the benchmark found to survive (provenance census record). Zero-shot, models reach around 60–70% on the longer-evidence sets and under about 60% on ExpertQA; fine-tuning on NLI-related data helps, fine-tuning on AttributionBench raises the average by 9.0% in distribution and 4.6% out, and "Simply switching stronger models cannot significantly improve the performance" (project page). Appending questions and responses to the input "is not the key to solving this task," and prompt engineering "only brings limited gain over 7 test sets" (project page). Of more than 300 error cases, a majority stem from the model's inability to process nuanced information and from the gap between what the model and the annotators can see (arXiv:2402.15089): over 66% from fine-grained information insensitivity, and about 26.8% from the mismatch of accessible information, which "brings into question the reliability of labels within current attribution evaluation datasets," the types tabled at 66.0%, 15.6% and 11.2% (project page). The project page states the limits of its evidence and its result: "The references are usually manually extracted from webpages by human annotators based on what they think is useful," and "there is still a large room for improvement" (project page). The Capture Registry records that the census record carries neither the 66% nor the 27% figure and that they are unchecked (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29); both stand on the project page (project page). The archive's account of the class begins from the same distinction the benchmark tests: frameworks of this kind "ask whether generated claims are supported by cited sources," while the Provenance Erasure Rate asks "what fraction of source-dependent composition occurs without any attributional return," so that existing work "evaluates citation quality where citation is attempted" and PER measures the failure to attempt attribution, "an attrition metric rather than a verification metric" (#716). #716 tables what support metrics miss, "Whether all source-dependent claims are cited," calls PER "complementary to, not competitive with, existing metrics," and reports the generative-search audit in which only 51.5% of generated sentences were fully supported by citations and 74.5% of citations supported their sentence (#716). In #725 the line runs between support and lineage: RAG faithfulness "asks whether an answer is supported by retrieved sources," semantic provenance whether it "preserves the lineage" of the meaning it uses, and "A faithful RAG answer can have high PER if it summarizes accurately while stripping authorial framework membership"; citation precision asks whether cited sources contain the cited claim, PER whether the lineage survived "even if no formal citation is made" (#725). #725 places attribution scores as "Industrial-grade infrastructure for support" whose semantic-provenance-aware variants "are not yet standard" and records, as a hypothesis for later compositions, that support and lineage be told apart (#725); #95 holds that the infrastructure for attribution evaluation "already exists in the research literature" and "can be extended" (#95). At this entity the census record states the same line in its own words, "evidence support is not credit to the original author" (provenance census record), which the Capture Registry calls "the line between this entity and the next" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29); #1611 lists attribution survival beside "the citation-recall and faithfulness metrics of retrieval-augmented evaluation" as a convergence for which "No priority is claimed" (#1611). #141 sets attribution and faithfulness metrics, which "measure whether generated statements are supported by and attributed to their sources," beside PER's rate of attribution failure at claim grain, and asks of them a further question it marks unmeasured: "whether the attribution failure is power-conditioned" (#141). The audits of citation support are read as a starting point: "a convincing sentence and a supporting citation are separate achievements" (#1695), and citation recall and precision are checked "apart from whether the territory and its operations survive" (#1705). #1695 adds the entity question support leaves open: "Local support must therefore be read alongside the identity of the object to which the answer attaches it. A set of true statements can compose a false identification" (#1695); and #1680 states that "A high attribution score with a distorted identity fails this packet's central test" (#1680). AttributionBench is a different entity from AttriBench: the census record's tag reads "NOT AttriBench: it asks whether evidence supports a claim, not who wrote a quote," and records the neighbour's context as "quote attribution, author, suppression, Berman et al., 2026" (provenance census record). The census places it in the lineage of answer engines, records the operation it tests as "generation with citations by search-augmented models," and asks of every entity "What provenance does this system carry, through which operation, on whose assertion, with what evidence of survival?", each field's quote "verbatim from a saved source" (provenance census record). Wikipedia has no article: the title returns "Wikipedia does not have an article with this exact name," and a search of article space for the name reports "There were no results matching the query." (Wikipedia, 2026-10-29). At its bare name on Google's AI Overview, signed out, on 2026-10-29, the Capture Registry records the entity identified "from the paper and its repositories," its task and headline figure the census record's quotes from the project page, checked against the census record and its saved pages, and AttriBench "respected by silence" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29). It records the benchmark "composed at full grain from its own paper" and "its makers are left in the cards": the four authors named in the arXiv and Hugging Face cards, neither they nor the OSU NLP Group in the answer, and no card citing the record that landed the same day (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

v0.9 §0.5: the first diff is small and ontological at one point. T and the field agree on the entity (a benchmark of whether generated claims are supported by their cited evidence) and T composes it at full grain. What T leaves out are the makers and the limits: the authors' own statement that the labels' reliability is in question, that the evidence is what annotators extracted, and the zero-shot qualifier on the low scores; and it reads a gap of access as a gap of understanding. The benchmark stands without the people who made it and without the caveats they attached to it.
